Follow the four shaping steps in order (set boundaries, rough out the elements, address risks and rabbit holes, then write the pitch), beginning by setting broad boundaries on the discussion before proposing solutions.
Respond to any raw idea with a soft 'maybe some day' that keeps options open, never an immediate yes/no or a backlog entry, because saying yes to everything creates an ever-growing pile.

Narrow the problem before designing: dig past the literal request to find where the user's workflow actually breaks down, flipping 'What could we build?' to 'What is really going wrong?', and asking a requester when and in what situation they wanted it rather than why or what it should look like.

Keep a poker face on unshaped ideas (neither shutting them down nor showing enthusiasm that sets expectations you may not meet) and let the appetite govern how much research is worthwhile, walking away from problems that are not critical and cannot yet be grasped.

Reject grab-bag efforts (vague redesigns, refactorings, or '2.0' projects) that are not driven by a specific problem, and never kick off work without a clear definition of what 'done' looks like; reframe such work around a concrete problem or split it into smaller problem-driven projects.
Treat boundary-setting as complete only when a raw idea, an appetite, and a narrowed problem definition are all in hand, before moving on to design the solution's elements.

Give the rough early design stage an explicit name and a deliberately coarse tool, and avoid producing specific mockups in shaping, because concrete mockups (especially from someone senior) bias downstream work; shaping output is guard rails, not a spec.

After roughing out elements, stress-test and de-risk the concept: a single unaddressed hole can derail a fixed-time project, so hunt rabbit holes by walking use cases in slow motion and questioning each part (never-done work? assumed fit? assumed a design exists? a hard decision to settle?), aiming for a thin-tailed risk profile of independent, well-understood parts.

Do not assume a team will 'figure it out': validate during shaping that a viable approach exists, and when a part hides a deep design problem, dictate a simplifying trade-off in the concept rather than pushing a tangled knot to the team under deadline, optimizing for basic quality and risk reduction over the ultimate design and calling out such patches explicitly in the pitch.

Ruthlessly minimize waste: create only the design artifacts genuinely needed to move the team's learning forward, use small batches, and treat anything in the process that does not improve outcomes as waste to be removed.

Keep a project within its appetite by explicitly declaring specific use cases out of bounds and cutting exciting-but-unnecessary parts down to nice-to-haves, because teams naturally try to cover every case.

Before writing up a pitch, walk the concept past technical experts framed as 'just an idea', ask 'is this possible within the appetite?' rather than 'is this possible?', actively hunt for time bombs, and keep the concept malleable by rebuilding it live and inviting radical simplifications.

Write every pitch with the five ingredients (problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, and no-gos), always pairing a problem with its solution: never pitch a solution with no problem (no fitness test) and never bet on a problem with no solution (unshaped work), and define the problem as a single specific story of why the status quo fails.
State the appetite inside the pitch as part of the problem, and add just enough concreteness for a low-context reader to get the idea without wireframes or high-fidelity mocks that box in designers.

In the pitch, list explicit no-gos (functionality intentionally excluded to fit the appetite) and increase visual detail only for a linchpin element everyone must see, with a disclaimer preserving designers' latitude.

Default to asynchronous communication and move to real time only when it is truly needed: post pitches for stakeholders to read on their own schedule, and use comments to poke holes or add information rather than to decide.

Do not keep a backlog: replace the central pile with decentralized lists each person or department tracks independently (none a direct input to betting), cross-pollinated by occasional one-on-ones, trusting that genuinely important ideas come back on their own.

Choose a cycle length that is long enough to finish something meaningful yet short enough to feel the deadline from the start (six weeks at Basecamp), reject too-short sprints whose planning overhead outweighs their output, and add a cool-down (about two weeks) between cycles for slack, bugs, and planning.

Treat a project that misses its cycle as a shaping failure and reframe it on the shaping track rather than pouring in more time, and rely on the hard deadline (with a real chance of not shipping) to motivate teams to own trade-offs.

Treat a bet as a real bet, not a plan: it has a defined payout (something meaningful finished, not time filled with tasks), it is a commitment to give the team the entire uninterrupted time working exclusively, and it caps the downside so the most you can lose is the amount bet.

Honor a bet by never interrupting or pulling the team away ('just a few hours' still breaks it), because momentum is second-order (the wrong hour can kill a day, a day a week); absorb new issues by waiting at most until the next cycle and betting only one cycle ahead, reserving interruptions for rare true crises.

Do not treat bugs as automatically urgent: judge by severity, reserve dropping everything for true crises, and handle the rest without interrupting cycles (fix in cool-down, pitch a large bug to the betting table, or run an occasional dedicated bug-smash cycle).

Match cycle expectations to where you are in the product's arc: an existing product follows the standard shape-bet-build flow, while a brand-new product moves through three phases (R&D, production, cleanup), still betting one cycle at a time.

In R&D mode, accept that you cannot shape reliably in advance: bet time on spiking key pieces with fuzzy shaping, staff the team with senior people who hold the vision (because early architecture defines the holes future features fit into), do not expect to ship, and decide cycle by cycle whether to continue.

Flip to production mode once the core architecture is settled: shaping becomes deliberate again, multiple teams can run in parallel, and 'shipping' means merging into the main codebase (not customer release), which keeps you free to cut features from the final cut as long as the team knows.

In the final pre-launch cleanup phase, drop the structure (no shaping, no fixed team boundaries, continuous small merges) but keep discipline: work only genuine must-haves, cap cleanup at two cycles, and let leadership make final-cut decisions, since a smaller V1 means less to answer for, support, and maintain.

At the betting table, keep problem and solution separate and weigh problems against each other (there are always more than time allows); treat a too-complicated or sweeping solution as a sign the problem is not understood specifically enough, and look for 80 percent of the benefit from 20 percent of the change.

Interrogate appetite and solution at the betting table without doing design there: when a stakeholder balks at the time, add problem context or probe whether the real objection is the solution; remember interface elements carry an invisible cost (screen real estate you cannot reuse); and pull back to the high level rather than debating design for more than a moment.

Hand over whole projects, not tasks: never let anyone act as a taskmaster who shreds the project into pieces; trust the team to define its own tasks and approach within the pitch's boundaries, because a team that owns the whole adjusts to what only becomes visible while doing the work, whereas up-front task assignment blinds people to that reality.

Organize work by the structure of the project into scopes (integrated front-end and back-end slices that can be finished independently), not by person or role, capturing granular tasks first and factoring them into scopes (tracked as to-do lists) only after real work reveals the true interdependencies; scopes then become the project's shared language.

Treat 'done' as deployed within the cycle so testing and QA happen inside it (respecting the circuit breaker), while leaving thin-tailed follow-ups such as docs, marketing, and announcements for cool-down; kick off by posting the shaped concept and holding a Q&A call.

Respect the orientation phase: expect the first days to look like nothing is happening as people learn the system and find a starting point, do not demand early status (it drives exploration underground), empower people to say 'I am still figuring out how to start', and only check in if the silence has not broken after about three days.

Expect the real work to be discovered, not imagined: the bulk (and hardest part) of a project is the tasks found by doing real work, so figure out what is needed by building, but start on something meaningful and central that is still small enough to finish end-to-end in a few days.

Adopt the method incrementally: start with a single six-week experiment (shape one project conservatively, guarantee one designer and two programmers uninterrupted time, present a pitch, hand over task discovery, and get one piece done) and prove success on one team before converting the wider organization; alternatively enter through shaping or through cycles.

Get one piece done early: rather than building toward a master plan that only converges at the 11th hour (lots done, nothing really done), integrate vertically on one small slice within the first week so there is something tangible to click through, choosing the most central UI as the first slice because design without a backend or a backend without UI cannot be judged.

Program just enough for the next step: programmers need not wait for design (the pitch gives enough direction for foundational modeling), they need only affordances (endpoints) rather than pixel-perfect screens, back-end work can be strategically patchy, and the team uses the cheapest thing that unblocks learning when the omitted work teaches nothing about the problem.

First make it work, then make it beautiful: resolve font, color, spacing, and layout only after raw affordances are wired and tested, because early uncertainty is about whether it works and makes sense; set up an iterative exchange between design and programming over one piece rather than one big hand-off.

Choose what to build first by three criteria (core, small, and novel): jump straight into the middle where the interesting problem is and stub everything else, and prefer the novel option among core-and-small candidates because it eliminates the most uncertainty.

Judge whether scopes are well drawn: they are right when you can see the whole project with nothing worrying hidden, conversations flow, and you always know where a new task goes; redraw them when done-ness is unclear (unrelated tasks), the name is generic ('front-end', 'bugs' signalling too little integration), or they are too big, and file bugs under the specific scope they affect.

Adapt scoping to the work's shape: for layer cakes (thin, even back-end) integrate design and code in one scope and judge by UI surface; for icebergs (lopsided back-end or UI) factor the UI out and split complex back-end into separate scopes to integrate in stages; and always question an iceberg's complexity before accepting it as necessary.

Keep a skeptical 'Chowder' list for loose tasks (more than three to five items means a scope is hiding), and mark nice-to-haves with a leading tilde so the team continuously separates must-haves from optional work and can cut the constantly growing scope.

Actively hammer scope by interrogating each new item (must-have? could we ship without it? what if we don't? new or pre-existing? how likely? which customers, core or edge? actual impact? aligned with the audience?), capturing must-haves as tasks a scope is not done without and marking nice-to-haves with a tilde as do-if-time items that usually get cut.

Do not measure status by counting tasks or by numeric estimates: to-do lists grow as work is discovered, and the same estimate means different things for familiar versus never-done work, so shift the focus of status to what is unknown versus what is solved.

Use the hill metaphor to communicate status: every piece of work has an uphill phase (figuring out the approach, full of unknowns) and a downhill phase (execution), 'percent complete' is meaningless until the top of the hill, and each scope is plotted on the hill so scopes give the language and the hill gives the state.

Make status self-serve and surface stuck work without blame: let the team position scopes on the hill and let managers compare past states to see what is moving versus stuck; because nobody wants to admit being stuck (hiding the biggest risks), treat a dot that does not move as a raised hand and keep the conversation about the work, not the person.

Diagnose a stuck scope before assuming failure: it may simply be badly drawn (several unrelated parts), so break it into independently movable scopes; and do uphill work with your hands, not just your head (thought about it, then validated the approach, then built enough to trust there are no other unknowns), since backsliding means a scope was called solved from a mental theory.

Sequence work by risk like a journalist's inverted pyramid: push the scariest, most uncertain scopes uphill first and get the critical unknowns over the top early, leaving routine screw-tightening for last, because work expands to fill the available time and nasty surprises must not surface at the end of the cycle.

Decide when to stop by comparing down to the baseline, not up to an ideal: shipping on time means shipping something imperfect, so judge good-enough by whether the work already beats how customers cope today, framing the call as customer value ('better than what they have now') rather than personal perfection, while still not lowering standards.

Use the fixed deadline to force trade-offs: before accepting any 'wouldn't it be better if' or new edge case, ask 'is there time for this?' and question new work before accepting it as necessary, expecting the team to actively make trade-offs rather than cram.

Treat variable scope as differentiation, not quality reduction: making choices about what to execute and how far makes the product better at some things than others; stay extremely picky about quality while asking which things actually move the needle for the core use cases.

Put QA at the end of the cycle to hunt edge cases outside the core and treat it as a level-up, not a gate every piece of work must pass: designers and programmers own the basic quality of their own work (programmers write their own tests) and do not depend on QA to ship quality.

Treat QA-discovered issues as nice-to-haves by default (collected separately, only triaged must-haves dragged onto the affected scope), and treat code review the same way, not a required check-point that blocks shipping but a 'makes it better' teaching opportunity used when there is time.

Extend a project past its deadline only rarely, and only when the remaining tasks are true must-haves that survived scope hammering and all remaining work is downhill (no unknowns); treat any uphill work left at cycle end as a shaping hole and reshape the project instead, preferring to enforce the appetite because habitually running into cool-down signals a shaping or performance problem.

After shipping, let the storm pass and stay debt-free: expect requests, bugs, and pushback, stay cool and avoid knee-jerk changes, and answer incoming feedback with a gentle 'no' rather than commitments, because saying yes takes future freedom like debt; more work on that area needs a new bet.

Treat customer feedback as unshaped raw input to the Set Boundaries step: if a request is truly important, make it a top shaping priority for the next cycle (betting other work to build) and schedule the shaped version later, rather than acting on it immediately.

When adopting the method, separate the universal basic truths from the scale-dependent specific practices: it takes real work to figure out the right work (or the universe forces the trade-offs later in a rush); be deliberate about what you bet on and cap the downside whatever the timeframe; and distinguish knowns from unknowns to sequence work and reserve capacity, regardless of organization size.

Scale the structure to the team: a team of two or three can drop cycles, cool-down, pitches, and the betting table and alternate shaping and building fluidly (being deliberate about which hat they wear), while a growing team should adopt six-week cycles, cool-downs, and a formal betting table, dedicating someone to shaping and protecting the core build team from interruption with separate support and infrastructure teams.

Get out of the deliverables business: refocus stakeholder conversations and team effort from producing hand-off documents to achieving customer outcomes, because documents do not solve customer problems and detailed spec deliverables are often celebrated and then never acted upon.

Measure progress by explicitly defined business outcomes rather than outputs (features and services), and reframe conversations around measurable business goals, because a feature's efficacy is largely speculation until it is live in the market.

Get out of the building (GOOB): resolve debates about user needs with real customers in the marketplace rather than in internal meeting rooms, and put ideas in front of customers far earlier than traditional practice.

Value making over analysis: build a rough first version of an idea rather than debating its merits in a conference room, because the hardest questions are answered by customers in the field, not internally.
Favour learning first and scaling second: prove an idea is right before scaling it to the whole user base, since scaling an unproven idea wastes time and resources if it fails.

Adopt Lean UX first as a mindset rather than a fixed set of tactics, adapting its practices to context (green-field versus established products) and ensuring the team has the psychological safety to share rough, unfinished work.
Embody the heart of Lean UX by designing no more than necessary, delivering it rapidly, and staying in close enough contact with customers to learn from real feedback quickly.
Treat the Lean UX techniques as one continuous process loop and cycle through it as often as possible, refining the team's thinking with each iteration.

Integrate Lean UX into Scrum's structure by using its events as mileposts so the whole team works on the same thing at once: write user stories as end-user benefits, actively groom the prioritized backlog as the primary tool for staying agile, and run end-of-sprint retrospectives to iterate the process as much as the product.

Include UX fully in an Agile transition and use honest retrospective feedback to repair the process, because a developer-driven Waterfall-to-Agile shift fails without UX and surfacing the team's real pain points triggers the dialog that produces genuine cross-functional collaboration.
Recognize that Lean UX is also a management method, so realizing its full benefit requires organizational change that each organization must adapt for itself through close collaboration.

Reject design heroism and ego-driven stars: avoid rockstars, gurus, and ninjas who do not share (they break the cohesion that shared understanding depends on), do not let glossy deliverables bias decisions or drive awards, hiring, and compensation, and remember that no single hero owns success, so Lean UX needs broad collaboration and treats each design as a hypothesis, which dethrones heroism because many ideas will fail and leaves only customer insight untouchable.

Adapt Lean UX to agency constraints: agencies are hard because clients pay for deliverables, hero-design culture is strong, and phase-based processes reinforce silos, and the client's 'throw it over the wall' expectation limits collaboration to biased critique, so make it work by maximizing client-agency collaboration and shifting focus from outputs to outcomes, including moving from fixed-scope deliverable contracts to time-and-materials or outcome-based contracts.

In environments with strict documentation standards for compliance, do not circumvent them (which causes rework, delays, and dissatisfaction); instead 'lead with conversation and trail with documentation' by running Lean UX practices early and then, as hypotheses are proven and directions solidify, producing the required documents for their intended purpose of capturing decision history and informing future teams, without letting them prevent the right product decisions.

Apply Lean UX beyond startups, including in enterprises: overcome 'we are not a startup' resistance by bringing in an outside coach to reinforce the internal message and introducing a system that helps teams internalize the steps, and make the change a little fun to reduce resentment about changing old habits.

Frame Lean UX as the evolution of product design that blends the best interaction-design techniques with the scientific method (combining Lean Startup, Agile software development, and design thinking) to remove bloat and uncertainty and push product design toward an objectively grounded result that is easy to use, beautiful, and measurably successful.

Write hypotheses in a structured, testable format ('We believe X; we will know we are right when we see [market feedback]') and, when a hypothesis is too big, decompose it into subhypotheses ('We believe [feature] for [persona] will achieve [outcome]; we will know when we see [signal]'), keeping each statement tied to a single outcome.
Compose hypotheses from three raw materials — target outcomes, personas, and candidate features — and make outcomes specific by breaking high-level outcomes into smaller predictive behaviours.

Define success with balanced criteria anchored to a prior benchmark: capture the current state of the success metrics before writing hypotheses, and include qualitative signals such as delight, recommendations, and sharing alongside quantitative measures.

Prepare inputs before an assumptions exercise: analytics on current usage, usability findings on why customers act, the history of past fix attempts, the stakeholder's impact analysis, and competitive analyses.

After launch, continuously harness organization-wide customer intelligence: mine customer-service agents (ask what they hear, hold monthly trend meetings, include them in design, and embed hypotheses in call scripts), onsite feedback channels (forms, forums, and communities, noting they skew to engaged customers), search logs (findability signals, validated via test pages), and site analytics and funnel analyses (usage, drop-off, and unbiased measurement of a launched experiment's outcome).

Start the assumptions exercise from a problem statement that focuses the team and defines constraints, using a three-part template (current goals; the observed gap and its business impact; and a 'how might we improve X for [measurable criteria]' request that does not dictate a solution); teams starting from scratch can still proceed but should expect slower consensus.

Sketch proto-personas on a four-quadrant sheet (sketch with name and role, behaviour-predicting demographics, needs and pain points, and candidate solutions), and narrow a brainstormed set to three or four target personas differentiated by needs and roles rather than demographics.

Make features serve the needs of the business, customer, and user rather than starting from a feature and justifying it backward; brainstorm candidate features as a team (sticky notes grouped into themes) aimed at driving the desired customer behaviour.

Work at low fidelity in collaborative sessions (sketches and wireframes), because low fidelity keeps the work malleable and makes it much easier to pivot when tests reveal the approach is not working.

Iterate up to a shared vision before raising fidelity: work in real time with teammates, rough things out at the lowest responsible fidelity, and increase fidelity only once the team understands and has bought into the concept, remembering that a shared vision empowers independent work and its absence shows as feature arguments, a sense of not moving fast enough, or rehashing the same issues.

Make conversation the primary means of communication and hold design conversations early and often, because it aligns the team and surfaces cross-disciplinary insight sooner and enables parallel work (for example engineers starting back-end infrastructure while the design is still being refined), which is the fastest route to an actual experience.

Use a Design Studio (Design Charrette) to bring the cross-functional team into one space to visualize solutions, break down silos, and build collaboration trust, and treat the ritual as adjustable because the goal is solving problems with colleagues, not following specific steps.

Run a Design Studio through its five phases (problem definition and constraints, individual divergent sketching, presentation and critique, iterate and refine, and team convergence), sized for five to eight people and split into multiple comparing teams when larger.

Expand the designer's role to whole-team facilitation and leadership: treat product design as a business-wide, whole-team discipline in which the designer opens up and facilitates the process (for example leading a Design Studio) and non-designers are invited to use design methods, rather than plugging designers into a waterfall 'design phase' to produce wireframes and specs, which narrows their scope and reinforces silos.

Prefer cross-functional over single-discipline collaboration: single-discipline work yields single-faceted ideas and forces documentation-heavy handoffs, whereas cross-functional collaboration puts everyone on the same page and the same level with no discipline dictating, a link between team cohesion and problem-solving productivity that is even supported by research.

Design the physical workspace for collaboration: co-locate teams in open, visible, accessible spaces seated in cross-functional groupings with abundant wall and whiteboard surface and breakout rooms, and when co-location is not possible provide video conferencing, smart boards, and occasional in-person meetings that noticeably improve morale.

Increase client-agency collaboration by pulling clients into the process earlier and more frequently, constructing check-ins around less formal milestones, and running joint work sessions, and keep software-development partners as active collaborators throughout the project (starting development as early as possible) rather than outsiders brought in at the end of a design phase.

Structure critique to be constructive: time-box each presentation to about three minutes, require presenters to state the persona and pain point, demand clarifying critique ('how does this address the problem?') rather than vague dislikes, and ensure every member both presents and receives feedback.

Maintain a style guide (pattern library) as a living collection of every customer-facing component (interactive, visual, and copy), because it creates efficiency: developers build approved core UI without waiting for a designer, designers stop recreating existing work, mundane placement debates disappear, and reviews focus on the core product challenge.

Treat the style guide as a maintained living process rather than a static artifact: dedicate people and time, assign an owner or curator (rotated regularly because the role is thankless), and make it easier to use than to avoid so compliance is easy.

Document each style-guide element with what/where/when detail: for interaction elements give appearance (sizes, constraints, styling), usual placement and exceptions, and when to use it over an alternative, and include visual elements and codified copywriting with the same detail.

Ensure the style guide is accessible, continually improved, and actionable: findable, distributable, searchable, and usable; kept malleably up to date; and functioning as a 'widget factory' that offers each element on demand as code plus graphical and wireframe assets, serving developers (via code snippets) as well as designers.

Prefer a wiki for the style guide because it is familiar to developers, keeps revision histories for UI rollbacks, and tracks changes with comments that capture rationale and speed onboarding; a live style guide that shares the application's code is closer to self-maintaining but adds infrastructure and process burden and still needs curation.

Choose a style-guide build strategy by product maturity, using the big-bang approach (document all UI at once) for young or simple products and the slow-drip approach (add elements as created) for legacy or complex products, and build it in two parts: a structured table of contents, then populated content.

Use lightweight non-prototype MVP techniques to test demand and value: email (open, click-through, and completion rates), Google AdWords (which language resonates and how much click interest exists), a landing-page facade with one clear call-to-action (each completed action counts as validation), and a 'button to nowhere' (clicks signal desire while you explain and capture feedback).

Treat MVP-test design as a creative process best served by a mashup of methods, including a Concierge MVP that manually delivers the service behind a minimal front end until a preset demand threshold justifies building the real back end.

Validate with research that is lightweight, continuous, and collaborative: build bite-sized research into every sprint rather than a big-bang study, and distribute research across the whole team (eliminating the researcher-to-team handoff to increase learning quality and shared understanding); if a trained researcher is available, use them as a coach rather than an outsourced doer.

Run a lightweight weekly testing rhythm (for example '3-12-1': three users seen by noon once a week) with a clear weekly structure of recruiting and planning, refining the MVP and moderator script, testing (no more than an hour per customer with the whole team observing), and deciding next steps, to keep the whole team continuously involved and minimize the time from concept to customer feedback.

Evolve toward a minimally viable testing process that fits your team and scales cheaply: keep only the moderator with the user while others watch remotely, debrief immediately, bring recruiting in-house, and use improvised low-cost equipment, which can deliver high-volume, fully-covered testing at a fraction of the cost of outsourced studies.

Plan weekly user validation and test for value before usability: schedule user sessions every week so the team is never more than five business days from validation, use ideation artifacts as the test material, test raw low-fidelity ideas for value first (do people want it?), and only test usability with higher-fidelity artifacts once desire is established.

Simplify the test environment: a lab is unnecessary when you have a quiet space, a networked computer, a webcam, and recording and broadcasting software, and broadcasting sessions to absent teammates and stakeholders spreads customer understanding across the organization while having the whole team watch cuts later debriefs and creates firsthand learning.
Where possible, offload the time-intensive work of recruiting, scheduling, screening, and replacing no-show participants to a third-party recruiter (roughly $75 to $150 per participant).

Handle contradictory feedback by looking for patterns (multiple instances worth exploring) and treating non-pattern data as outliers to park in a backlog rather than ignore or over-serve, and verify an uncertain single-channel signal against other channels, treating non-corroboration as a sign the sample may be skewed.

Exploit the continuous cadence to detect trends over time: seeing only a few users each week leaves some questions open across weeks but surfaces gradual shifts in attitudes, so ask a fixed set of level-setting 'vital signs' questions in every session so signals that seem anecdotal become powerful in aggregate.

Once hypotheses have evolved into working code, use A/B (or A/B/n) testing by releasing to a small subset against a control cohort and keeping changes small enough that any behavioural change can be attributed directly, and if a variant does not move the needle, engage that audience directly to learn why.

Organize work into themes and feed Scrum from collaborative ideation: group a series of sprints under a theme, kick it off with team brainstorming and validation to build a backlog of ideas, run a shorter pre-sprint brainstorm to refresh the next backlog from the latest insight, and bring co-created kickoff artifacts into the iteration planning meeting to write, evaluate, and prioritize user stories together.

Require the whole team to participate in all Agile activities, because a discipline that does not participate has its concerns left out of plans; cross-functional participation enables smart backlog sequencing (for example a designer flagging a design-heavy story to buy lead time), preserves shared understanding (the relevant slice of any meeting saves downstream explanation), and is how each role negotiates the time it needs.

Guarantee designers protected creative time within the cadence, because concurrent two-week design-and-development cycles rarely provide it; deliberately carve out creative time within a Scrum sprint or adopt a more flexible flow-based method such as Kanban.

Adjust deliverable weight to collaboration bandwidth: when you must collaborate remotely with a less-available development team, expect to produce heavier deliverables while still iterating your way up to higher fidelity.

Adopt 'competencies over roles' and actively dismantle silos: let members contribute secondary competencies in any discipline where they have expertise and interest, because job-title gatekeeping is deeply anticollaborative and silos breed waning cross-discipline conversation, mistrust, finger-pointing, and cover-your-ass behaviour.

Value and reward problem-solving over sexy deliverables: promote fast thinking and shared-understanding-building alongside aesthetics, and seek out and reward designers who can illustrate the path they took from idea to validated learning to experience.

Track and pay down UX debt the way teams treat technical debt: commit to continuous UI improvement by writing backlog stories that capture the gap between the current and desired experience and advocating for them, because framing rework as debt gets it consistently prioritized.

When part of the work is outsourced to a third-party development vendor (where Lean UX is more likely to break down because contractual relationships resist its required flexibility), structure the engagement on a time-and-materials basis and plan for the change that learning will inevitably cause.

Be pragmatic in a resistant environment: when managers feel threatened by the new way of working, ask forgiveness rather than permission and prove value with quantifiable wins such as time and money saved, and if leadership persistently refuses to see the value and the organization stays on a path of 'blind design,' consider alternative employment.

Design AI-infused systems on the assumption that they operate under uncertainty and will produce false positives and false negatives; make the interaction resilient to mistakes rather than assuming correct behavior, because unpredictable AI behavior otherwise erodes user confidence and drives abandonment.
At first contact, make the AI system's capabilities explicit so users understand what it can and cannot do and form an accurate mental model (Guideline 1).
Make it easy to edit, refine, or recover when the AI is wrong, and build in safeguards such as verification steps for consequential actions (Guideline 9).

Organize human-AI design guidance by the interaction phase in which it applies (initially, during interaction, when the system is wrong, and over time) to make the guideline set easy to apply and reason about.
Reject the automation-versus-augmentation false choice; integrate AI algorithms with interface design so the system amplifies, augments, and empowers people.
Design AI systems to amplify human ability while keeping humans, their goals, and their responsibility at the center of the system.
Communicate how well the system performs, including how often it may be wrong, so users can calibrate trust; use hedging language and explicit quality expectations (Guideline 2).
Time when the system acts or interrupts to the user's current task and environment (Guideline 3).
Show information relevant to the user's current task and environment rather than uniform or stale content (Guideline 4).
Deliver the experience in a way that fits users' social and cultural context and their expected interaction norms (Guideline 5).
Ensure the system's language and behavior do not reinforce unfair stereotypes or biases, and use diverse evaluators and bias-detection tools to surface issues (Guideline 6).

Do not treat conformance to the guidelines as sufficient for fairness or ethics: a system can satisfy every guideline and still harm people or their livelihoods, so deliberately evaluate broader societal impacts and use diverse evaluators to surface issues invisible to majority groups.
Make it easy to invoke or request the system's services when the user needs them (Guideline 7).
Give users efficient, always-available means to directly invoke and to terminate automated services.
Make it easy to dismiss or ignore undesired AI services, keeping them unobtrusive and easy to scroll past or turn off (Guideline 8).
When uncertain about the user's goals, disambiguate or gracefully degrade rather than acting confidently, weighing the expected costs, benefits, and uncertainty before automating (Guideline 10).
Explicitly represent and reason about uncertainty in the user's goals and focus of attention rather than assuming they are known.
Let users access an explanation of why the system behaved as it did, scaling the explanation effort to the decision's stakes (Guideline 11).
Maintain short-term memory of recent interactions and let users efficiently refer back to it (Guideline 12).
Personalize the experience over time by learning from the user's actions (Guideline 13).
Maintain a working memory of recent interactions so users can make natural, efficient references to their shared short-term context.
Limit disruptive changes when updating or adapting the system's behavior, avoiding jarring, unexpected shifts (Guideline 14).
Let users give preference feedback during normal interaction, such as like/dislike or mark-as-important controls (Guideline 15).
Immediately convey how a user's action will affect the system's future behavior (Guideline 16).
Show users the automated system state and likely near-future behavior before requiring them to rely on the system.
Provide global controls that let users customize what the system monitors and how it behaves, kept distinct from instance-level feedback (Guideline 17).
Inform users when the system adds or updates its capabilities, especially changes that require their attention (Guideline 18).

Phrase each guideline as a short, verb-first rule of action of roughly 3-10 words with no conjunctions and a one-sentence clarifying description, splitting compound guidelines so each can be independently judged as applied or violated.

When curating a guideline set, keep only concepts that are AI-specific, concrete enough to design for, and observable at the interface; discard guidance that is too vague, too scenario-specific, not AI-specific, or actionable only at the AI-modeling layer.

Treat a general guideline set as a starting point rather than a complete solution: general guidelines may not fully cover systems without graphical interfaces (voice assistants, wearables) or high-risk, highly regulated domains (semi-autonomous vehicles, robot-assisted surgery, financial systems), which can require additional specialized guidance.

Treat the guidelines as a shared, reusable resource for designing and evaluating AI-infused systems, and communicate each one with concrete, anonymized examples of both its application and its violation so practitioners can recognize it in real interfaces.

Before treating a guideline set as authoritative, validate it empirically: run a heuristic-evaluation-style study in which experienced practitioners find both applications and violations of each guideline across a maximum-variance sample of real products, after familiarizing them with one application and one violation per guideline and rating each guideline's clarity.

Consider a guideline set broadly relevant when evaluators can find at least one application or violation of every guideline across a wide variety of product categories, while expecting weaker signal for products whose interaction is primarily image-, sensor-, or voice-based rather than graphical UI and text.

When auditing products against guidelines, protect the reliability of the counts: recruit experienced evaluators (at least a year of HCI/UX work and familiarity with discount usability methods), assign roughly 2-3 evaluators per product spanning a range of experience, clean the data by removing duplicates and reclassifying misused 'does not apply' responses, and use a two-pass inter-rater review that discards cases where reviewers disagree.

Read guideline-audit counts as prioritization signals: applications plus violations indicate a guideline's overall relevance; many applications relative to violations indicate it is widely implemented; many violations relative to applications indicate it is relevant but under-implemented and thus a design opportunity; and many 'does not apply' responses flag scope or observability issues rather than irrelevance.

When two guidelines are systematically confused (four or more cross-confusions or repeated clarity complaints), revise them with parallel wording that sharpens the intended distinction, for example: what the system can do versus how well it does it versus why it acted; current context versus personalization learned over time; short-term memory versus long-term learning; and instance-level feedback versus global control.

Refine guideline wording with an expert review by UX/HCI practitioners familiar with discount usability methods and adopt the revisions experts find clearer, while accepting that some inherently close pairs (such as what the system can do versus how well it does it) may remain somewhat hard to distinguish.

Coordinate interface design with model development: given a model's expected performance, choose designs that reduce costs while maximizing user benefit (for example, offer multiple options until the model is accurate enough to act proactively), and resolve trade-offs where guidelines conflict, such as conveying the consequences of user actions versus actively learning from behavior in complex models.

Design mixed-initiative interfaces that couple automated reasoning with direct manipulation instead of choosing one over the other; never use complex automation to paper over poor design, and never restrict to direct manipulation where automation adds real power.

Apply the Prometheus Principles as the core interface rules for human control over automation: (1) consistent interfaces so users can form, express, and revise intent; (2) continuous visual display of the objects and actions of interest; (3) rapid, incremental, and reversible actions; (4) informative feedback acknowledging each action; (5) progress indicators; and (6) completion reports confirming accomplishment.
Introduce automation only where it delivers genuine value beyond what the user could already accomplish with direct manipulation alone.
Keep automation perceptible and documented to users; hidden automation is a defect because imperceptible AI is not ethical AI.
Do not name, label, or market automation beyond its actual capability, because overstated capability lowers user vigilance and invites over-trust.
Choose actions by weighing the context-dependent costs, benefits, and uncertainties of acting, and take autonomous action only when its expected utility for the user exceeds that of inaction.

Make outcome utilities, and hence the action threshold, context-sensitive: raise the threshold when the cost of unwanted action grows (e.g., the user is deeply focused elsewhere) and lower it when that cost falls (e.g., ample screen space) or when the cost of inaction rises (e.g., the user is rushed).

Derive an action threshold p* by equating the expected utilities of acting and not acting (from the four goal-by-action outcome utilities); at run time simply compare the inferred goal probability against that threshold, acting above it and refraining below it.
Infer the probability that the user holds a given goal from observable evidence using a classifier trained by watching the user, and key the system's response to that inferred probability.

Treat asking the user as a first-class third action alongside acting and doing nothing: model dialog inside the same expected-utility framework so that two thresholds (inaction-to-dialog and dialog-to-action) decide whether to do nothing, ask, or act, and weigh the cost of needlessly interrupting before asking.

Allow thresholds to be assessed directly: provide sensible default utilities and thresholds, but let designers or users set the two key thresholds (or supply their own outcome utilities) directly, since directly assessed thresholds still imply an underlying expected-utility model.

Model the temporal pattern of user attention (e.g., fit dwell-time preferences from observed behavior as a function of a task feature such as message size) and apply it either by making outcome utilities time-dependent or by deferring service until the user is likely ready.

Gracefully scale the precision or scope of service to match current uncertainty, preferring to do less but correctly; when a precise parameter cannot be resolved, fall back to the most relevant coarser scope rather than a precise but likely-wrong guess.

Assume users will often want to finish or refine the agent's work: place the user in an approximately correct starting state to cut interaction and navigation effort, and provide efficient means to collaborate on refining the result.
Minimize the cost of the system's inevitable poor guesses through appropriate time-outs and natural gestures for rejecting an offered service.
Endow agents with socially appropriate default behaviors and courtesies befitting a benevolent, unobtrusive assistant.
Keep learning from observation over the system's lifetime, continuing to improve both the user model and the timing model to better serve the user's goals.

Derive training labels implicitly from user follow-through (e.g., mark an item relevant when the user takes the corresponding action within a predetermined time horizon) and collect behavioral signals such as dwell time to incrementally refine the models.
Let users control the adaptation policy by specifying the schedule on which the system incrementally refines its learned models.

Layer assistance as a service over an existing direct-manipulation application: detect a newly focused item, infer the task it implies, and pre-fill structured fields for the user to review, edit, and save.
Decouple human control from automation and design for high levels of both at once, rather than treating them as a single trade-off.

Place each task deliberately in the framework: full computer control only for rapid-action, well-understood tasks; full human mastery where the doing itself is the value; high-control-plus-high-automation for complex, poorly-understood tasks.
Actively design against both danger zones: excessive automation (which hides failure modes and erodes oversight) and excessive human control (which permits avoidable deadly mistakes).
Prefer incremental refinement of proven automations over leaping to full autonomy, especially where full autonomy is not yet demonstrably safe.
Use automation for routine tasks rather than higher-level cognitive functions, and keep that automation transparent.
Retain manual override controls for authorized humans even in highly automated systems, so operators can correct or supersede the automation when needed.
Design against automation-induced de-skilling and vigilance decrement: preserve the human skills and attention that will be needed when the automation fails.
Model human control and computer automation as independent design dimensions instead of treating autonomy as a one-way replacement for control.
Treat human control and computer automation as independent design dimensions, and deliberately look for high-automation designs that still preserve meaningful human control.

Match design rigor, oversight, and human-in-the-loop to the application's consequence tier: light for low-stakes consumer tools, stronger for consequential medical/legal/financial systems, strongest for life-critical systems.
Prevent excessive-control mistakes with well-designed interlocks, guards, and software range-checking that bound unsafe or irreversible actions.
Preserve user control even in low-stakes automation and limit malicious manipulation, since better user control both raises satisfaction and reduces misuse.
Add constraints, interlocks, and review mechanisms that mitigate both unchecked automated action and unchecked human action.

Engineer reliability through concrete technical practices: audit trails and near-miss analysis, accepted benchmark verification and validation, continuous data-quality and bias review, and stakeholder-confidence design.
Engineer safety through open management that builds a culture of safety: leadership commitment, channels to report problems, internal review of failures and near misses, and public failure reporting.

Deliver Reliable, Safe & Trustworthy systems by combining sound technical practice (reliable), open safety-culture management (safe), and well-designed independent oversight (trustworthy), with failure and near-miss monitoring driving continual improvement.
At the organization level, build a safety culture through leadership commitment, safety-oriented hiring and training, failure reporting, internal review boards, and alignment with industry practices.
Earn trust through respected independent oversight structures, and hold designs to the standard of being trustworthy rather than merely trusted.

At the industry or public-stakeholder level, use independent oversight such as regulation, external audits, insurance accountability, civil-society input, and professional standards to strengthen trust.
Design computers to support people (reducing workload, raising performance, ensuring safety), not as teammates, partners, or companions that endear themselves emotionally.
Keep human accountability visible by designing computers as controlled support systems, not as entities that appear to own decisions or responsibilities.
Guard against algorithmic hubris and design for drift: assume data, user behavior, and context will change, and monitor for the resulting model decay.
Make systems comprehensible, predictable, and controllable, in line with convergent industry and academic human-AI guidelines, because these properties raise self-efficacy and yield RST systems.
Expect interface decisions built on these principles to involve genuine tradeoffs with no default right answer, so budget for careful study, creative design, and rigorous testing.
Make meaningful human control and human values explicit design requirements, not after-the-fact interface additions.
Continuously monitor deployed designs with domain experts to detect problems and refine them after release.
Let users express intent through visual interfaces by default, but provide auditory and haptic alternatives where they suit the situation or users with disabilities.

Choose interaction modalities by task demands: use speech when hands or eyes are unavailable, and prefer persistent information-rich visual displays for dense, spatial, comparative, or ongoing status information.
Guide design choices explicitly by the consequences and reversibility of the mistakes a system can make.
Treat human responsibility for mistakes as a design driver, using detailed audit trails and consistent machine-state feedback to enable rapid retraining of users and redesign of systems.
Evaluate human-centered AI by human outcomes, stakeholder effects, user experience, and technical performance together.
Evaluate AI designs by human outcomes such as self-efficacy, creativity, clear accountability, social participation, privacy, security, fairness, reliability, safety, and trustworthiness.
Use concrete social-benefit goals, such as SDG-aligned outcomes, to guide AI design when the system affects public welfare or community outcomes.
Choose the application-specific balance among human mastery, machine control, and high-control/high-automation support, and block configurations that create operational risk.
Select AI design metaphors deliberately because metaphors shape product expectations, authority allocation, and policy discussions.
Prefer augmenting designs such as supertools or active appliances when the product goal is to expand human ability rather than replace human agency.
For consequential automation, structure interaction as outcome preview, alternative comparison, deliberate user initiation, and visible execution monitoring.
Provide accessible equivalents whenever previews or control panels rely on visual presentation.
Translate AI ethics commitments into concrete governance across engineering reliability, management safety culture, independent oversight, and public regulation.
Translate responsible-AI ethics into concrete governance at the team, organization, and industry levels instead of stopping at abstract principles.
Treat reliability, safety, and certification as separate governance responsibilities that require technical practices, organizational management, and external accountability.
Revisit HCAI principles as practice, industry context, and technology change rather than freezing them as universal one-time rules.
Include foreseeable misuse and harm categories in HCAI design and governance reviews.
Do not default to human-like agents, teammates, or robots; first consider tool-like, tele-operated, supervisory, or appliance-like designs that exploit machine strengths.
For supervisory work, provide compact spatially stable displays, predictable alerts, modest highlights, and user-configurable layouts that support situational awareness without seizing control.
Support shared awareness and mutual assistance for fast-moving operations by making user activity and system state easy for nearby or collaborating operators to monitor.
Use public language and imagery that communicates tools, appliances, tele-operation, user interfaces, and human responsibility rather than autonomous humanoid intelligence.
When aiming at broad societal goals, pair technology design with behavioral change and explicitly align the system with human-centered development outcomes.
